cards.q: Define the standard electrode potential, \(E^{\ominus}\), of a half-cell.
cards.a: The emf of a cell made from the half-cell connected to a standard hydrogen electrode, measured under standard conditions.
cards.why: The standard hydrogen electrode is given a potential of exactly 0.00 V, so the cell emf is the potential of the other half-cell.

cards.q: What are the standard conditions for measuring \(E^{\ominus}\)?
cards.a: Temperature 298 K; gas pressure 100 kPa; every ion at a concentration of \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.why: The potential depends on these conditions, so they must be fixed for values to be compared.

cards.q: How are half-equations written in a table of standard electrode potentials (the IUPAC convention)?
cards.a: As reductions, with the electrons on the left, e.g. \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Zn(s)}\), \(E^{\ominus} = -0.76\ \text{V}\).
cards.why: Each half-equation is an equilibrium; the sign of E tells you how readily it goes in the reduction direction.

cards.q: Describe the standard hydrogen electrode.
cards.a: Hydrogen gas at 100 kPa bubbled over a platinum electrode (coated with platinum black) dipping into a solution of \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ions at \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) (e.g. hydrochloric acid), at 298 K.
cards.why: Half-equation: \(\mathrm{2H^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons H_{2}(g)}\); its potential is defined as 0.00 V.

cards.q: Explain why a reference electrode is needed to measure electrode potentials.
cards.a: The potential of a single half-cell cannot be measured; only the potential difference between two half-cells can.
marks: A voltmeter needs two connections, so it can only measure a potential difference between two electrodes.
So each half-cell is measured against the same reference half-cell, the standard hydrogen electrode.
The reference is assigned 0.00 V, giving every other half-cell a value on the same scale.

cards.q: Why is platinum used as the electrode in a half-cell with no solid metal, such as the hydrogen electrode?
cards.a: Platinum is inert (it does not react) and it conducts electricity, so it provides a surface for electron transfer.
cards.why: Platinum black (finely divided platinum) has a large surface area, so equilibrium is set up quickly.

cards.q: How is a half-cell set up for (a) a metal and its ions, and (b) a non-metal gas and its ions?
cards.a:
(a) A clean strip of the metal dipping into a \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solution of its ions, e.g. Cu in \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)}\).
(b) The gas at 100 kPa bubbled over a platinum electrode in a \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solution of its ions, e.g. \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) with \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}(aq)}\).
cards.why: Every half-cell is then connected to a standard hydrogen electrode at 298 K.

cards.q: How is a half-cell set up for ions of the same element in different oxidation states, such as \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\)?
cards.a: A platinum electrode dipping into a solution containing both ions, each at \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.why: There is no solid metal in the half-equation, so an inert electrode is needed to carry the electrons.

cards.q: What is a salt bridge, and what does it do?
cards.a: Usually filter paper soaked in saturated potassium nitrate solution. It connects the two solutions.
marks: It completes the circuit by allowing ions to move between the two half-cells.
This keeps each solution electrically neutral as the reaction proceeds.
Potassium nitrate is used because its ions do not react with, or precipitate, the ions in the half-cells (KCl would precipitate silver ions as AgCl).

cards.q: True or false: electrons flow through the salt bridge from one half-cell to the other.
cards.a: False. Electrons flow through the external wire; ions move through the salt bridge.
cards.why: Electrons cannot travel through a solution; the salt bridge carries charge by the movement of ions.

cards.q: Describe how to measure the emf of a cell made from a copper half-cell and a zinc half-cell.
cards.a: Make the two half-cells, join the solutions with a salt bridge and the electrodes to a high-resistance voltmeter.
steps: Clean the metal strips with emery paper; place Zn in \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}(aq)}\) and Cu in \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)}\).
Connect the solutions with a salt bridge of filter paper soaked in saturated potassium nitrate.
Connect the electrodes with wires to a high-resistance voltmeter and record the reading at 298 K.
cards.why: The voltmeter has a high resistance so almost no current flows: the concentrations do not change and the full emf is measured.

cards.q: Write the conventional cell diagram for a cell made from a zinc half-cell and a copper half-cell, and say what each line means.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Zn(s)\,|\,Zn^{2+}(aq)\,||\,Cu^{2+}(aq)\,|\,Cu(s)}\)
A single line is a phase boundary; the double line is the salt bridge.
cards.why: The more negative half-cell (where oxidation happens) is written on the left; in each half-cell the species are written in the direction of the reaction.

cards.q: How is \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) calculated from the electrode potentials of the two half-cells?
cards.a:
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{right}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{left}}\)
or \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{positive}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{negative}}\)
cards.why: With the cell written conventionally, the right-hand electrode is the positive one and the emf is positive.

cards.q:
Calculate \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) for \(\mathrm{Zn(s)\,|\,Zn^{2+}(aq)\,||\,Cu^{2+}(aq)\,|\,Cu(s)}\).
\(\mathrm{Zn^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Zn}\) \(E^{\ominus} = -0.76\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Cu}\) \(E^{\ominus} = +0.34\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +1.10\ \text{V}\)
steps: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{right}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{left}}\)
cards.why: Copper, the more positive half-cell, is the positive electrode; zinc is oxidised.

cards.q: A cell is made from a copper half-cell (\(E^{\ominus} = +0.34\ \text{V}\)) and a silver half-cell (\(\mathrm{Ag^{+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Ag}\), \(E^{\ominus} = +0.80\ \text{V}\)). Write the cell diagram and calculate the emf.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cu(s)\,|\,Cu^{2+}(aq)\,||\,Ag^{+}(aq)\,|\,Ag(s)}\); \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.46\ \text{V}\)
steps: Silver has the more positive potential, so it is the positive electrode: write it on the right.
cards.why: Copper is oxidised and silver ions are reduced; the potential of the silver half-cell is not doubled even though 2 Ag⁺ react per Cu.

cards.q: Write the cell diagram for a standard hydrogen electrode connected to an \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}\) half-cell (\(E^{\ominus} = +0.77\ \text{V}\)).
cards.why: A comma separates two species in the same phase. The platinum electrodes go on the outside. On the right, the oxidised form \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) comes first because it is being reduced.

cards.q: A nickel half-cell is connected to a standard copper half-cell (\(E^{\ominus} = +0.34\ \text{V}\)). The emf is 0.59 V and copper is the positive electrode. Calculate \(E^{\ominus}\) for \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Ni}\).
cards.a: \(E^{\ominus} = -0.25\ \text{V}\)
steps: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{positive}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{negative}}\), so \(0.59 = 0.34 - E^{\ominus}_{\text{Ni}}\)
cards.why: Any standard half-cell of known potential can act as a reference once its value is known.

cards.q: In the cell \(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,|\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,||\,Cu^{2+}(aq)\,|\,Cu(s)}\), which electrode is negative, and which way do electrons flow in the external circuit?
cards.a: Magnesium (\(E^{\ominus} = -2.37\ \text{V}\)) is the negative electrode. Electrons flow through the wire from Mg to Cu.
cards.why: Magnesium is oxidised, releasing electrons; \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions gain them at the copper electrode. \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.34 - (-2.37) = +2.71\ \text{V}\).

cards.q: What is an electrochemical series?
cards.a: A list of half-equations (written as reductions) in order of their standard electrode potentials.
cards.why: It ranks oxidising and reducing agents by strength, so it can be used to predict reactions.

cards.q: In an electrochemical series, where are the strongest oxidising agent and the strongest reducing agent found?
cards.a:
Strongest oxidising agent: on the left of the half-equation with the most positive \(E^{\ominus}\).
Strongest reducing agent: on the right of the half-equation with the most negative \(E^{\ominus}\).
cards.why: From the data booklet: \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\) in acid (+1.77 V) is the strongest oxidising agent listed; Na (−2.71 V) is the strongest reducing agent.

cards.q:
Use \(E^{\ominus}\) values to decide whether chlorine will oxidise bromide ions.
\(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2Cl^{-}}\) \(+1.36\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{Br_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2Br^{-}}\) \(+1.09\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: Yes. \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2Br^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-} + Br_{2}}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.27\ \text{V}\).
steps: Chlorine is reduced and bromide is oxidised.
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{reduced}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{oxidised}} = 1.36 - 1.09 = +0.27\ \text{V}\)
The emf is positive, so the reaction is feasible.
cards.why: The half-equation with the more positive potential goes forwards (reduction); the other goes backwards (oxidation).

cards.q:
Will iodine oxidise iron(II) ions to iron(III)?
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}}\) \(+0.77\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{I_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2I^{-}}\) \(+0.54\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: No. \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.54 - 0.77 = -0.23\ \text{V}\), which is negative.
steps: For \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) to oxidise \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\): iodine is reduced, iron(II) is oxidised.
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.54 - 0.77 = -0.23\ \text{V}\): not feasible.
The reverse is feasible: \(\mathrm{2Fe^{3+} + 2I^{-} \rightarrow 2Fe^{2+} + I_{2}}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.23\ \text{V}\).
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is the stronger oxidising agent of the two, so it oxidises iodide.

cards.q:
Write the overall equation, and calculate \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\), for the reaction of acidified manganate(VII) with iron(II) ions.
\(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} + 8H^{+} + 5e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Mn^{2+} + 4H_{2}O}\) \(+1.51\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}}\) \(+0.77\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} + 8H^{+} + 5Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_{2}O + 5Fe^{3+}}\); \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.74\ \text{V}\)
steps: Manganate(VII) has the more positive potential, so it is reduced; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + e^{-}}\).
Multiply the iron half-equation by 5 to balance the electrons, then add.
cards.why: Electrode potentials are never multiplied when a half-equation is multiplied.

cards.q:
Write the overall equation, and calculate \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\), for the oxidation of iron(II) ions by acidified dichromate(VI).
\(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 6e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_{2}O}\) \(+1.33\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}}\) \(+0.77\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 6Fe^{2+} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_{2}O + 6Fe^{3+}}\); \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.56\ \text{V}\)
steps: Six electrons are gained by one dichromate ion, so six iron(II) ions are oxidised.
cards.why: Always check that atoms and charges balance in the final equation.

cards.q: How can you tell from \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) whether a redox reaction is feasible?
cards.a: Calculate \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{(species reduced)}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{(species oxidised)}}\). If it is positive, the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.
cards.why: Equivalently: the oxidised form in the more positive half-equation will oxidise the reduced form in the more negative one.

cards.q: True or false: when a half-equation is multiplied by 2 to balance electrons, its \(E^{\ominus}\) value is also doubled.
cards.a: False. \(E^{\ominus}\) values are never multiplied.
cards.why: An electrode potential is a property of the half-cell (energy per unit charge), not of the amount reacting.

cards.q: Explain how the electrode potential of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Zn(s)}\) changes if \([\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]\) is lowered below \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\), and the effect on the emf of a zinc–copper cell.
cards.a: The zinc electrode potential becomes more negative, so the emf of the cell increases.
marks: Lowering \([\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]\) shifts the equilibrium to the left (Le Chatelier).
More zinc atoms release electrons, so the electrode becomes more negative.
The difference between the copper and zinc potentials increases, so \(E_{\text{cell}}\) increases above 1.10 V.

cards.q: Why are the conditions important when measuring an electrode potential?
cards.a: Each half-cell is an equilibrium. Changing a concentration, a gas pressure or the temperature shifts that equilibrium and so changes the potential.
cards.why: So a measured \(E\) only equals \(E^{\ominus}\) at 298 K, 100 kPa and \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) ions.

cards.q: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) is positive for a reaction, but no reaction is seen. Give two reasons.
cards.a: The reaction may be too slow (kinetic inhibition), or the conditions may not be standard.
marks: The activation energy may be very high, so the rate is too slow to observe (the reaction is kinetically inhibited).
\(E^{\ominus}\) values apply only at standard conditions; real concentrations, pressures or temperatures can change the potentials enough to change the prediction.
\(E^{\ominus}\) values predict feasibility only; they say nothing about rate.

cards.q:
Show that acidified manganate(VII) should oxidise water to oxygen, and suggest why its solutions are nevertheless stable for long periods.
\(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}/Mn^{2+}}\) \(+1.51\ \text{V}\); \(\mathrm{O_{2} + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2H_{2}O}\) \(+1.23\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.51 - 1.23 = +0.28\ \text{V}\), so the reaction is feasible, but its activation energy is so high that it is extremely slow.
steps: Manganate(VII) is reduced; water is oxidised to oxygen.
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.51 - 1.23 = +0.28\ \text{V}\): positive, so feasible.
The solution does not visibly change: the reaction is kinetically inhibited.
cards.why: A positive emf means a reaction can happen, not that it happens at a noticeable rate.

cards.q: \(\mathrm{MnO_{2} + 4H^{+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Mn^{2+} + 2H_{2}O}\), \(E^{\ominus} = +1.23\ \text{V}\); \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2Cl^{-}}\), \(E^{\ominus} = +1.36\ \text{V}\). Explain why \(\mathrm{MnO_{2}}\) does oxidise concentrated hydrochloric acid to chlorine.
cards.a: Under standard conditions \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = -0.13\ \text{V}\), but the high concentrations shift both equilibria and make the reaction feasible.
marks: Under standard conditions \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.23 - 1.36 = -0.13\ \text{V}\): not feasible.
High \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) shifts the \(\mathrm{MnO_{2}}\) equilibrium to the right, making its potential more positive.
High \([\mathrm{Cl^{-}}]\) shifts the chlorine equilibrium to the left, making its potential less positive.
The emf becomes positive, so the reaction occurs (helped by heating and loss of chlorine gas).

cards.q: How is \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) related to the total entropy change and to the equilibrium constant, \(K\), of a reaction?
cards.a: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) is directly proportional to \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) and to \(\ln K\).
cards.why: \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = R \ln K\). A positive \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) means \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) is positive and \(K > 1\).

cards.q: What do a large positive \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) and an \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) close to zero each tell you about the extent of a reaction?
cards.a:
Large and positive: \(K\) is very large, so the reaction goes almost to completion.
Close to zero: \(K\) is close to 1, so an equilibrium mixture of reactants and products forms.
cards.why: \(\ln K\) is proportional to \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\), so even a few tenths of a volt correspond to a very large \(K\).

cards.q:
Use \(E^{\ominus}\) values to show that copper(I) ions disproportionate in aqueous solution.
\(\mathrm{Cu^{+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Cu}\) \(+0.52\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Cu^{+}}\) \(+0.15\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2Cu^{+}(aq) \rightarrow Cu(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq)}\); \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.37\ \text{V}\), so feasible.
steps: One \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) is reduced to Cu (\(+0.52\ \text{V}\)); another is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) (reverse of the \(+0.15\ \text{V}\) half-equation).
Positive, so the disproportionation is feasible.
cards.why: In disproportionation the same species is both oxidised and reduced.

cards.q: How can \(E^{\ominus}\) values show whether a species X will disproportionate?
cards.a: Find the half-equation in which X is reduced and the one in which X is formed by reduction (so X is oxidised in reverse). If \(E^{\ominus}\)(X reduced) is more positive than \(E^{\ominus}\)(X formed), \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) is positive and X disproportionates.
cards.why: E.g. \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.77 - 0.68 = +1.09\ \text{V}\) for \(\mathrm{2H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O + O_{2}}\).

cards.q: Name the three types of commercial electrochemical cell, and give an example of each.
cards.a: Non-rechargeable (e.g. an alkaline battery), rechargeable (e.g. the lithium-ion cell in a mobile phone), and fuel cells (e.g. hydrogen–oxygen).
cards.why: In a non-rechargeable cell the reaction cannot be reversed; in a rechargeable cell it can; a fuel cell is supplied with fuel continuously.

cards.q: Explain how the electrode reactions in a cell generate an electric current.
cards.a: Oxidation releases electrons at the negative electrode; they flow through the external circuit to the positive electrode, where reduction takes place.
marks: At the negative electrode, a species is oxidised and releases electrons.
The electrons flow through the external circuit (doing work, e.g. powering a phone) to the positive electrode.
At the positive electrode, a species gains the electrons and is reduced; ions move within the cell to balance the charge.

cards.q: Give the simplified electrode reactions in a lithium cell while it is being used.
cards.a:
Positive electrode: \(\mathrm{Li^{+} + CoO_{2} + e^{-} \rightarrow Li^{+}[CoO_{2}]^{-}}\)
Negative electrode: \(\mathrm{Li \rightarrow Li^{+} + e^{-}}\)
cards.why: Overall: \(\mathrm{Li + CoO_{2} \rightarrow Li^{+}[CoO_{2}]^{-}}\). Cobalt is reduced from +4 to +3.

cards.q: Given \(\mathrm{Li^{+} + CoO_{2} + e^{-} \rightarrow Li^{+}[CoO_{2}]^{-}}\), \(E^{\ominus} = +0.56\ \text{V}\), and \(\mathrm{Li^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Li}\), \(E^{\ominus} = -3.04\ \text{V}\), calculate the emf of the cell, and give the reaction at the negative electrode during recharging.
cards.a: emf = 3.60 V. On recharging: \(\mathrm{Li^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Li}\) at the negative electrode.
steps: Recharging applies an external voltage that reverses both electrode reactions.
So lithium ions are reduced back to lithium at the negative electrode.
cards.why: In a rechargeable cell the products stay on the electrodes, so the reactions can be driven backwards.

cards.q:
A rechargeable nickel–cadmium cell uses:
\(\mathrm{NiO(OH) + H_{2}O + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Ni(OH)_{2} + OH^{-}}\) \(E^{\ominus} = +0.52\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{Cd(OH)_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons Cd + 2OH^{-}}\) \(E^{\ominus} = -0.88\ \text{V}\)
Deduce the overall reaction when the cell is used, and its emf.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cd + 2NiO(OH) + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow Cd(OH)_{2} + 2Ni(OH)_{2}}\); emf = 1.40 V
steps: The more positive half-equation goes forwards (reduction of NiO(OH)); cadmium is oxidised at the negative electrode.
Double the nickel half-equation to balance electrons, then add; the \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions cancel.
cards.why: On recharging, both reactions are reversed.

cards.q: What makes a storage cell rechargeable?
cards.a: Its electrode reactions can be reversed by applying an external voltage greater than the cell’s emf, because the products stay in contact with the electrodes.
cards.why: Electrode potentials give the voltage of each cell; cells are joined in series to make a battery of higher voltage.

cards.q: What is a fuel cell?
cards.a: A cell in which the energy released when a fuel reacts with oxygen is used to generate a voltage. Fuel and oxygen are supplied continuously, so it does not need to be recharged.
cards.why: Hydrogen, methanol and other hydrogen-rich fuels are used.

cards.q: Give the electrode reactions in an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
cards.a:
Negative electrode: \(\mathrm{H_{2} + 2OH^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O + 2e^{-}}\)
Positive electrode: \(\mathrm{O_{2} + 2H_{2}O + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 4OH^{-}}\)
cards.why: Overall: \(\mathrm{2H_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O}\). The electrolyte is aqueous KOH or NaOH.

cards.q:
Calculate the emf of an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
\(\mathrm{O_{2} + 2H_{2}O + 4e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 4OH^{-}}\) \(E^{\ominus} = +0.40\ \text{V}\)
\(\mathrm{2H_{2}O + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons H_{2} + 2OH^{-}}\) \(E^{\ominus} = -0.83\ \text{V}\)
cards.a: emf = 1.23 V
steps: Oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode; hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode.
cards.why: It is the same as for the acidic cell, because the overall reaction is the same.

cards.q: Give the electrode reactions in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte.
cards.a:
Negative electrode: \(\mathrm{H_{2} \rightarrow 2H^{+} + 2e^{-}}\)
Positive electrode: \(\mathrm{O_{2} + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.23 - 0.00 = 1.23\ \text{V}\). \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ions move through the electrolyte from the negative to the positive electrode.

cards.q: In a methanol fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, give the reaction at the negative electrode and the overall reaction.
cards.a:
Negative electrode: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}OH + H_{2}O \rightarrow CO_{2} + 6H^{+} + 6e^{-}}\)
Overall: \(\mathrm{2CH_{3}OH + 3O_{2} \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: The positive electrode reaction is \(\mathrm{O_{2} + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O}\). Methanol is a liquid, so it is easier to store and carry than hydrogen.

cards.q: Give the benefits and risks to society of using hydrogen fuel cells and lithium-ion cells.
cards.a: Both reduce the use of fossil fuels where they are used, but their materials and energy sources carry costs and hazards.
marks: Hydrogen fuel cells: the only product is water, and they convert fuel energy to electrical energy more efficiently than burning it.
But hydrogen is mostly made using fossil fuels or electricity, and it is flammable and hard to store and transport.
Rechargeable lithium-ion cells: reused many times, reducing waste; power phones, laptops and electric vehicles.
But lithium is flammable and cells can catch fire if damaged; mining cobalt and lithium has environmental and human costs, and used cells must be recycled safely.

cards.q: True or false: a fuel cell stores electrical energy, like a rechargeable battery.
cards.a: False. A fuel cell does not store energy; it converts chemical energy from a continuous supply of fuel into electrical energy.
cards.why: It works for as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied, and never needs electrical recharging.

cards.q: True or false: the larger \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) is, the faster the reaction.
cards.a: False. \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) shows how feasible a reaction is, not how fast it goes.
cards.why: Rate depends on the activation energy. A reaction with a large positive emf can still be very slow.
